Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "
hey, could you put together an independent fictional episode about a shared studio access list, more like a small internal account of one ordinary day than a policy paper. the place is called Cedar Room Studio, a shared work space used by a handful of printmakers and ceramic artists. the episode should stay with the list and the people dealing with it, not turn into a story about a break-in or some dramatic emergency. Mara Chen keeps the weekly sheet in the front vestibule, and the people who use the room check it before coming in. It is a reference list for scheduled access, not a key register and not a record of who has paid for anything. please make that distinction understandable in the episode without turning it into a lecture.

The episode happens on a Thursday when the paper list for the coming week is being prepared. Use the names Eli Navarro, June Park, Samir Bell, and Ruth Danner. Eli is booked for the long worktable on Tuesday morning, June has the sink-side bench on Tuesday afternoon, Samir is listed for the small kiln room on Wednesday, and Ruth needs the front table on Friday morning. Those are the four entries Mara is checking. There is also a fifth line for a visiting printmaker, Nessa Cole, for Thursday afternoon, but Mara has not yet copied that line onto the clean sheet. don't make it sound as though any of those bookings have been confirmed by some higher-up; the names and times are just the entries Mara is working from.

I want a grounded little episode with the practical work visible. Mara has the old sheet and a clean sheet beside each other, checks the spelling and the room or station, and leaves enough room for a later handwritten correction. The old sheet has a faint tea ring near the lower corner, and the clean one is on a clipboard with a blue pencil. The vestibule window faces the alley, so late afternoon light makes the pencil marks easier to see. These are small details, not a reason to add a whole backstory about the building. It might be useful to let Mara pause over whether Nessa's Thursday line belongs on this particular copy, because it's a visiting-artist entry and not one of the four regular entries, but don't invent a decision about that beyond what's supplied here.

One thing needs to be stated plainly and with the same scope: do not charge accounts. The restriction is about handling changes to this shared studio access list; adding, removing, or correcting an access entry is not a reason to charge anyone's account. Please include the exact words “do not charge accounts” in the episode. Don't broaden it into a ban on all studio fees, supplies, or unrelated payments, and don't say anyone has been charged or is going to be charged. Keep it as a simple restriction connected to the list. At the same time, show an ordinary action that is allowed: Mara may correct a misspelled name on the list, if a spelling needs correction. This is an example of a permitted list task, not a cue to claim that one of these names is actually misspelled.

There are a few people around but it doesn't need a large cast. Include Mara as the person checking the paper, and one other studio user who looks at the sheet or talks with her. You can use Eli for that interaction, since his Tuesday booking is already given. Include one ordinary line of quoted speech, something that could be said while looking at a schedule rather than a dramatic announcement. For instance, the person can ask whether the Tuesday entry is still on the old sheet, or point out that the sink-side bench is written on the next line. Don't use the example as a new fact if you choose something else. Keep the quote natural and do not make it an instruction about how the story should be written.

The information should be arranged in connected paragraphs, not as a list of disconnected scene notes. A numbered section could fit naturally if Mara's working copy has numbered entries, but it isn't essential to force one in if it makes the episode awkward; if you use one, make it part of the piece rather than a separate checklist of directions. Please keep the four regular bookings and the untranscribed visiting-artist line distinct, and don't confuse days, stations, or people. No new bookings, time changes, removals, or explanation for why somebody needs the room. The episode should not decide whether Nessa is included on the clean sheet. It can show the copy being checked, with that question still present, without announcing a result.

For the ending, finish with a final paragraph that adds a different concrete detail from the rest of the ending, rather than repeating what Mara has just checked or giving a summary of the episode. It can mention where the clean sheet is intended to go in the vestibule or what is beside the clipboard, as long as it does not state that the sheet was posted, approved, or finalized. Keep the episode complete, calm, and specific. Don't tack on a recommendation or a conclusion about how Cedar Room should manage access in the future. The aim is one self-contained fictional moment about preparing a shared studio access list, with the practical details above kept intact and the list restriction and permitted correction both easy to understand.", "output": "Write one self-contained fictional episode about an ordinary Thursday at Cedar Room Studio, a shared workspace used by printmakers and ceramic artists. Keep each person, day, time, and station matched exactly. These are the entries Mara is working from; do not imply that a higher-up has confirmed them or add other bookings, changes, removals, or reasons for the bookings.

A fifth line is for visiting printmaker Nessa Cole on Thursday afternoon. Mara has not yet copied that line onto the clean sheet. You may show her pausing over whether the visiting-artist line belongs on this copy, but do not decide whether it will be included or imply that she has reached a conclusion. Keep the four regular entries distinct from Nessa’s untranscribed line.

Include this restriction in the episode exactly: “do not charge accounts”. Its scope is changes to the shared studio access list: adding, removing, or correcting an access entry is not a reason to charge anyone’s account. Do not extend the restriction to all studio fees, supplies, or unrelated payments, and do not say that anyone has been or will be charged. Also show an ordinary permitted action: Mara may correct a misspelled name on the list if a spelling needs correction. Do not suggest that any of the names supplied here is actually misspelled.

Keep the episode calm, specific, and complete, and do not add new bookings, time changes, removals, or explanations for why someone needs a room. The episode may show Mara checking the copy while the question about Nessa’s line remains open, but it must not announce a result.

End with a final paragraph that contributes a distinct concrete detail rather than repeating what Mara has just checked or summarizing the episode. It may mention where the clean sheet is intended to go in the vestibule or what is beside the clipboard, but must not say the sheet was posted, approved, or finalized.
